title: Auriga Systems — LLM runway, batching & budget POC scoping
summary: POC kickoff to agree success criteria and run a 2-week benchmarking sprint focused on per-token unit economics, batching and KV/prefix caching gains; baseline synthetic traces, two model variants, and a pilot budget guardrail discussed.
topics: success criteria (latency p50/p95, throughput, token cost)
workload sizing and synthetic trace construction
benchmark plan: models, quantization, and measurement windows
batching & caching knobs and expected cost delta
budget constraints and runway (monthly token budget)
timeline and next steps for pilot
next_steps: Maya to share pilot pricing sheet + unit econ workbook and benchmark template (link) by 2027-11-17
Auriga to provide 3 representative request traces and average token stats by 2027-11-18
Carlos to propose two model configs (13B q4f16, 70B q4f16 fallback) and a staging benchmark plan by 2027-11-19
action_items: Maya Patel - send cost workbook and pilot SOW - due 2027-11-17
Priya Menon - export product traces (3000 requests sample) and schema - due 2027-11-18
Carlos Ruiz - create benchmark script + config and shared repo link - due 2027-11-19
Daniel Kwan - confirm data residency/VPC constraints and provide KMS contact if needed - due 2027-11-20
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-11-14 15:00 PST | Duration ~60m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Leah (CSM), Priya (Auriga PM), Daniel (Auriga Eng), Nina (Auriga CTO), Samir (SRE)

[00:00] Maya: alright good afternoon everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intros — i'm maya, i'm covering ae — carlos is our se and leah is cs. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya: hi maya, thanks — doing well. excited to get this scoped. we've been trying to get a realistic per token runway for Q1.
[00:13] Nina: hi all. our main ask today is: can we get to a predictable monthly cost per active user given our chat assistant workload? we want a pilot that proves that.
[00:22] Carlos: great, that's exactly what this scoping is for — we'll cover success metrics, the benchmark design, and the knobs onto batching/caching that drive unit economics.
[00:30] Daniel: quick context — production traffic profile is highly spiky; avg session length 3-4 turns, mean input tokens ~90, generated tokens ~280. tail latency is the thing that kills UX.
[00:40] Maya: perfect, that's helpful. is the traffic mostly text-only? attachments or retrieval ops?
[00:45] Priya: mostly text, but about 12% of sessions include a retrieval call for user docs — around 2–3 external calls per session.
[00:52] Carlos: ok that matters for effective tokens and end-to-end latency. can i ask about your runway — budget?"
[00:57] Priya: we have a soft cap of $25k/month for inference in the pilot phase, but we need a model where we can scale to $75k/month if usage ramps.
[01:05] Maya: ok good, budget guardrails. for unit economics we'll estimate per-inference token cost under different batching and caching configs and show runway ceilings. usually we split the POC into a 2-week bench sprint then a 4-week pilot.
[01:15] Samir: what's your recommended baseline model? we have options to run our own or use hosted. we care about throughput and cost.
[01:22] Carlos: for a first pass we usually test two variants: a smaller 13B quantized (q4f16) as the baseline for cost-sensitive, and a larger 70B-variant as a quality/fallback. the 13B tends to be around $0.0004–0.0008 per 1k tokens on our hosted tier raw compute before batching; with batching and prefix caching you'll often see effective costs halve for certain workloads.
[01:40] Priya: can you slow down on the numbers — 0.0004–0.0008 per 1k tokens?
[01:44] Carlos: sorry yes — i misspoke: that's per token units. typical hosted per-token compute cost (not including data egress) for 13B quantized might be ~0.0000004–0.0000008 per token, which converts to roughly $0.0004–$0.0008 per 1k tokens. depends a lot on model, quantization, and short-sequence inefficiencies.
[02:00] Daniel: okay that range helps. what's the impact of batching — we see high concurrency during drops — will batching hurt tail latency?
[02:07] Carlos: there's tradeoffs — with continuous batching our runtime adapts to maintain latency SLOs. For your workload we can test batch windows of 5ms, 20ms, 50ms. small windows keep p50 low but reduce batching gains; larger windows increase throughput and lower per-token cost but we need to measure p95 impact. in past retail customers saw ~30–45% per-token cost reduction moving from 5ms -> 50ms on similar traces.
[02:29] Maya: also remember KV/prefix caching — for repeated context (e.g., same user context across turns) we can avoid recomputing the prefix and only compute new tokens. that often subtracts 20–35% of compute for multi-turn sessions.
[02:42] Priya: our average session is 4 turns — that sounds promising. how do you simulate that in benchmarks?
[02:47] Carlos: we'll ask you for a representative sample of traces — a few thousand requests across light/heavy/attachment flows. we'll replay them in order to capture multi-turn cache hit patterns. the benchmark plan will include synthetic arrival processes to reproduce spikes.
[02:58] Nina: are there cases where caching would violate PII constraints? we have some sensitive documents.
[03:03] Maya: good call — caching is configurable and cache persistence can be disabled for sensitive flows. we also support per-request flags to avoid storing KV cache. for PII-heavy sessions you'd run without persistent cache. Carlos: note that removes those cost gains but you maintain control.
[03:16] Daniel: what about quantization quality delta — do we test ROUGE or human evals?
[03:20] Carlos: yes we'll include both automated metrics (perplexity, log-prob deltas) and a small human eval panel — 50–100 samples to compare QA and coherence. quality gates will be part of success criteria.
[03:30] Priya: can you outline the success criteria we should agree on now?
[03:34] Maya: sure — proposed success criteria: (1) p50 latency under 300ms for interactive flows, p95 under 1.5s on baseline 13B config; (2) per-inference median cost lower than $0.020 given your token mix (we'll compute exact); (3) caching/batching reduces per-token compute by >=25% for multi-turn flows; (4) quality delta vs your golden set within 3 points on the rubric (no regression).
[04:00] Priya: that p50/p95 targets are aggressive but realistic if batching/caching works. we might push p95 to 2s for the fallback model.
[04:08] Carlos: that's fair — we'll measure both. fallback policy: route to larger model for low-confidence outputs or certain intent classes; we can show blended economics.
[04:17] Samir: on deployment — we will likely need VPC/private deployment for production, but pilot can be hosted if data is obfuscated. is that acceptable?
[04:24] Maya: yes pilot hosted is OK, we offer private control plane options later. for the pilot we'll mirror your VPC network egress patterns in the bench but won't yet do a full private install.
[04:33] Daniel: what telemetry will you need from our side during the bench?
[04:36] Carlos: request logs with anonymized IDs, token counts, timestamps, input lengths, and whether the request used retrieval. we also want label signals for quality evaluation where available. a CSV or S3 dump is fine.
[04:45] Priya: we'll get that out. you mentioned runway math — can you sketch a quick per-active-user example?
[04:50] Maya: sure. if an active user averages 1 session/day, 4 turns, 370 total tokens per session => ~11k tokens/month per active user. at $0.02 per inference that's... sorry mixing units. If we assume effective token cost 0.0005 per token (example), 11k tokens ~= $5.50 per user/month. multiply by 3k MAU leads to ~$16.5k/month. We will produce exact workbook with your token distributions.
[05:17] Priya: awesome — that helps. can we see optimistic and pessimistic scenarios?
[05:21] Carlos: yes workbook will have low/med/high usage, and knobs for batching window and cache hit rate. we usually show sensitivity of cost to cache hit rate (0-80%).
[05:30] Nina: on bench models — what's the fallback to avoid outages? auto-fallback to smaller models or to degraded response?
[05:36] Maya: Redwood supports policy-based routing: by latency, cost, or model capacity. we can do fast-failover to a smaller model or to a canned low-quality response depending on thresholds. We'll test failover behavior in bench.
[05:47] Daniel: for the benchmark inputs, we have mixed-length prompts — some 2k token legal excerpts. will that break things?
[05:53] Carlos: long context increases memory and KV size; we'll test with truncated or windowed contexts and show cost delta. in private deployments we can extend sequence length with dedicated hardware but cost rises. we'll include a long-context test vector.
[06:05] Maya: timeline recap — proposed: this week (by 11/18) Auriga provides traces, Redwood provides bench configs and pricing workbook (by 11/19), bench kickoff 11/22, 2-week bench (11/22–12/06), bench readout 12/08, then pilot SOW and 4-week pilot starting mid-December.
[06:20] Priya: that cadence works. any blockers on our side?
[06:23] Daniel: need to confirm legal for sharing traces, but can anonymize. also want to know what security docs you'll send.
[06:30] Leah: i'll drop SOC2/ISO docs and an onboarding checklist in the shared folder. link: https://redwood.example/docs/security-pack (placeholder).
[06:36] Daniel: thanks. one more question on cost — how do reserved/dedicated capacity offers change unit economics?
[06:41] Carlos: reserved capacity lowers per-token compute for predictable, high-throughput steady-state. e.g., a reserved pool can reduce effective compute cost by 20–40% vs on-demand hosted. we'll model both hosted-on-demand and a projected dedicated pricing tier in the workbook.
[06:55] Priya: would love to see a projection if we hit 10k MAU.
[06:58] Maya: we'll include a 6-month runrate table with 1k/3k/10k MAU scenarios.
[07:04] Nina: about quality — human evals are expensive. can we do a small focused panel?
[07:08] Carlos: yes 50–100 paired comparisons usually surfaces regressions. we'll run automated metrics first to triage.
[07:14] Samir: benchmarking environment — do you need our keys or a sandbox?
[07:17] Maya: we'll provide a staging API endpoint and run replay tests; we won't need production secrets. for retrieval tests, you can provide sample docs in S3.
[07:26] Priya: ok practical items: we will anonymize traces, export to s3, and grant read access to carlos@redwood for benchmarking.
[07:33] Carlos: perfect. i'll also share the bench repo with docker configs and a perf dashboard.
[07:38] Maya: any other concerns?
[07:40] Daniel: just want to ensure we capture downstream RBAC needs — enterprise SSO is required eventually.
[07:44] Leah: noted — i'll attach SSO/SAML onboarding steps.
[07:48] Maya: great. recap of deliverables: redwood sends cost workbook and bench config, auriga sends traces; bench kickoff 11/22; two-week bench with mid-bench sync; readout and final SOW.
[07:59] Priya: that's a wrap, thanks everyone. looking forward to the workbook.
[08:03] Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invites and link to the shared folder.
[08:07] (call ends)

Notes about transcript: occasional mis-attributions (Speaker 2 shows up) and auto-time stamps every ~30–90s. references to links are placeholders.
